q: A company reports record sales, up 20 %, but earnings per share rose just 5 %. Is that a strong quarter?
why: Sales headlines can impress, but what counts is how much earnings per share grew versus the same quarter last year. A 5 % gain is far below what big winners showed before their runs.

q: Before their big runs, did most top-performing stocks show latest-quarter earnings growth averaging above 70 %?
why: In a study of 600 top stocks from 1952 to 2001, three out of four had latest-quarter earnings up more than 70 % on average. Most of the rest caught up the very next quarter.

q: Earnings jumped three quarters in a row, but sales grew only 5 %. Is that profit growth likely to last?
why: A company can lift profits for a while by trimming costs such as advertising or research. Lasting earnings growth needs rising sales behind it, ideally at least 25 % in the latest quarter.

q: A stock's P/E is near the low end of its usual range. Is that alone a good reason to buy?
why: The study of top winners found P/E did little to explain their moves. A low P/E usually has a reason, often weak earnings, and a stock at 8 times earnings can still fall to 4.

q: From 1953 to 1985, did the best stocks usually begin their big runs at a higher P/E than the Dow average?
why: Their average starting P/E was 20, while the Dow averaged 15, and the winners' P/Es grew to about 45 as they rose. Insisting on cheap P/Es would have ruled out most of them.

q: Is a return on equity of at least 17 % a common trait among the great growth stocks of the past?
why: Return on equity shows how well a company turns shareholders' money into profit. Nearly all the top growth stocks over 50 years had at least 17 %, and the very best had 25 % to 50 %.

q: Buying stocks far below their old highs feels safer. Did the study of winners find it works better than buying near highs?
why: Stocks on the new-high list tended to keep rising, while those on the new-low list tended to keep falling. What looks expensive to most people often climbs further, and what looks cheap often sinks.

q: In the study of top winners since 1880, did nearly all have something new behind them, like a product, leadership, or industry change?
why: More than 95 % of the standout stocks had at least one fresh driver: a new product or service, new management, or a shift in industry conditions. Something has to change for a stock to surge.

q: Before their biggest runs, were top stocks already outperforming most other stocks in price?
why: From the early 1950s through 2008, the best performers had an average relative strength of 87 before their big moves. They were already beating nearly 9 in 10 stocks when the run began.

q: A rival of a hot market leader sells a similar product, and its stock looks cheaper. Is it usually the better buy?
why: Investors often buy the cheaper copycat hoping the leader's success rubs off. History shows those followers rarely match the leader, because their profits usually fall short.

q: In a rising market, the index dips 10 %. Your two growth stocks fall 15 % and 35 %. Is the one down 15 % likely the stronger stock?
why: During a pullback in a rising market, the growth stocks that fall least are usually the best picks once they recover. A 35 % drop while the market loses 10 % is a warning sign.

q: Nearly every big fund already owns a stock. Does that make it a safer buy?
why: When almost all institutions hold a stock, the easy gains are often behind it, and those holders are a large pool of potential sellers. If trouble hits or the market turns, their selling can push the price down hard.

q: When a healthy stock pulls back in price, is it a good sign if trading volume dries up?
why: Light volume on a dip suggests few holders are rushing to sell. Rising volume on up days, by contrast, usually reflects institutions buying.

q: Is roughly half of a stock's price move tied to how its industry group and sector are doing?
why: Studies credit 37 % of a stock's move to its industry group and another 12 % to its broad sector. Checking the group before buying is worth the effort.

q: Bargain hunters like the weakest-ranked industry groups. Do stocks there tend to beat those in top-ranked groups?
why: On average, stocks in the top 50 or 100 groups did better than those in the bottom 100. The suggestion is to focus on the top 20 groups and skip the bottom 20.

q: Does a stock that led one bull market usually lead again in the next one?
why: Only about one in eight leaders from one bull market leads again in the next. The market tends to move on to new companies and new ideas.

q: In a healthy cup with handle, should the handle form in the upper half of the whole base?
why: A handle up high shows buyers already won back more than half of the earlier drop. Handles sitting in the lower half, or below the 10-week line, point to weak demand and fail more often.

q: The handle on a chart keeps creeping upward along its lows instead of dipping first. Is that a healthy setup for a breakout?
why: A good handle needs a small pullback that shakes out nervous holders. A handle that wedges up or drifts flat along its lows skips that cleanup and breaks out with much higher odds of failing.

q: After a big run-up, a stock rests sideways for weeks. Each dip stops higher than the last and daily moves shrink. Promising setup?
why: A rest of 2 weeks to 2 months with rising lows shows buyers absorbing every dip. Small, quiet days near the end suggest sellers are drying up just before a possible breakout.

q: During the rest, price slides below its rising 10- and 20-day averages and stays there. Is the setup still healthy?
why: In a healthy rest, price rides on top of the rising 10- and 20-day averages. Falling below them and staying there means the pause is no longer a strong one.

q: In a double bottom shaped like a W, is the buy point set at the top of the W's middle peak?
why: The pivot sits on the right side of the W, level with the middle peak, which should be a bit below the pattern's high. If the pattern has a handle, the handle's high sets the pivot instead.

q: A stock clears its pivot point on roughly average volume. Does that meet the volume you want on a proper breakout?
why: On a real breakout, volume should run at least 40 % to 50 % above normal. That surge usually means institutions are buying. Ordinary volume suggests big buyers are not behind the move.

q: You find a breakout late. The stock is already more than 10 % above its pivot. Is now still a sound time to buy?
why: Buying beyond 5 % to 10 % past the pivot is buying late. A normal pullback can then drop you below the 8 % loss limit and force a sale. Wait for the next proper setup instead of chasing.

q: On breakout day, is buying when price clears the high of the first minutes of trading a standard way to enter?
why: The opening range high, taken from the first 1, 5 or 60 minutes, gives a clear trigger. When price clears it on the day the stock breaks out, buyers are showing control right away.

q: A stock broke out a while ago and now trades far above its 10- and 20-day averages. Is buying here a good entry?
why: A stock stretched far from its short averages leaves no sensible nearby stop and poor odds. The better move is to let it go and wait for a new rest to form.

q: Can an index show distribution on a day it actually closes higher?
why: Distribution is heavy volume without real price progress. If volume rises but the index stalls with a much smaller gain than the day before, professionals may be quietly selling into strength.

q: During one four-week stretch, an index racks up five distribution days. Should that raise a warning about the market's direction?
why: When selling days pile up, four or five of them within four or five weeks, the general market very often turns down soon after. That is a signal to get more defensive.

q: On the second day of a rally attempt, the index jumps sharply. Is that usually the follow-through day you're waiting for?
why: The first few days of a rally prove little. Look for the follow-through from the fourth day on, most often days four to seven: a strong gain on higher volume than the day before.

q: After a confirmed follow-through day, can the new rally still fail within a few days?
why: A follow-through raises the odds, but it is not a promise. Large funds can push the averages up for a day. If real buyers don't return, the rally can collapse on heavy volume soon after.

q: The main index keeps setting new highs, but the advance-decline line stopped rising months ago. Is that a warning sign?
why: When the index climbs but fewer stocks join in, money is crowding into a shrinking group of big names. The breadth line has typically peaked five to ten months before the blue chips. A long divergence is a reason to get defensive.

q: Near a big market low, the index holds above its bottom while the advance-decline line keeps falling. Is that a bearish signal?
why: It is the opposite: a positive divergence. After a long decline, nervous buyers return to quality stocks first while speculative ones keep sliding. The longer this split lasts, the bigger the eventual turn tends to be.

q: Your stock is now 8 % below what you paid, but you still love the company. Should you keep holding until it comes back?
why: The 7 % to 8 % line is a hard limit. Liking the company doesn't change the math. Sell without waiting or hoping, and keep the loss small so one mistake can't turn into a big one.

q: Your stock is well above your cost, then dips 8 % from its peak. Does the loss-cutting rule require you to sell now?
why: The loss rule is measured from your purchase price, not from the high. With a solid profit in a bull market, you can give a stock room for a normal 10 % to 15 % pullback.

q: With $20,000 to $200,000 to invest, is owning four or five carefully chosen stocks a sensible number?
why: A small account does better with a few stocks you understand and can follow closely. The more names you own, the harder it is to keep track of them all.

q: Your stop belongs at today's low, but that low sits further from your entry than the stock's average daily range. Should you pass?
why: The stop goes at the low of the buying day. If that distance is wider than a normal day's movement, the risk is too big for the setup, so the trade is skipped.

q: Risking 1 percent per trade means you only put 1 percent of your account into each stock. True?
why: Risk is what you lose if the stop is hit, not the size of the position. With 0.25 to 1 percent at risk and a close stop, the position itself can be much larger.

q: After breaking out of a proper base, do many winning stocks rise about 20 % to 25 % before pausing?
why: A study of winners found they often climb 20 % to 25 % after the breakout, then pull back and build a new base. That pattern is why taking profits around that level makes sense for most stocks.

q: A fresh breakout gains 20 % in just two weeks. Should you hold it for at least eight weeks rather than cash in?
why: A stock that fast may be a true leader capable of much bigger gains. The exception to the 20 % profit rule: hold such a stock for at least eight weeks.

q: A breakout trade is working after a few days. Is selling part of it and moving the stop to your entry price the plan?
why: After 3 to 5 days, sell a third to a half. Moving the stop on the rest to your buy price means the trade can no longer turn into a loss.

q: Your remaining shares show a big gain but just closed below the 20-day average. Is the large profit a reason to keep holding?
why: The rest of the position rides only while price holds above the 10- or 20-day average. A close below is the exit signal, and a big gain is no reason to sit through a large drop.

q: After many months of gains, a stock posts its biggest one-day price jump of the whole run. Is that a sign to buy more?
why: In a stock already far extended from its base, the largest daily gain of the entire move tends to come very close to the peak. It is a warning to consider selling, not to add.

q: A stock that has run up for many months suddenly opens with a price gap above yesterday's close. Could that signal the top is near?
why: This is called an exhaustion gap. When a stock is greatly extended, usually at least 18 weeks out of an early base, a gap up at the open often marks the final burst of buying.

q: Earnings are rising and the news is exciting, but the stock churns sideways on heavy volume around a flattening average. Good time to buy?
why: That is a topping stage. Heavy, choppy trading means early buyers are cashing out into the excitement. A great story does not change the chart, and the reward-to-risk balance now works against a buyer.

q: A stock drops below its support into Stage 4, but volume is light. Should that breakdown still be treated as a real sell signal?
why: Upside breakouts need a volume surge to be trusted, but breakdowns do not. Many stocks slipped into Stage 4 on quiet trading and still fell hard. Heavy volume makes it worse; light volume is no reason to relax.

q: In a bear market, the index briefly pops above its 30-week average, but that average is still pointing down. Is this the all-clear?
why: A brief poke above a falling average is not enough. The defensive stance holds until the average itself stops declining and starts to level out. Until then, the main trend is still down.

q: Your market indicators flag a high-risk zone, though prices have not cracked yet. Is building a large cash reserve a sensible response?
why: High-risk zones are when false signals on individual charts multiply. Raising cash and becoming very picky about new buys protects you before the damage shows up in prices.

q: Many fear shorting because losses look unlimited. With a protective buy-stop in place, is a realistic worst case similar to a failed purchase?
why: A buy-stop above the short caps the damage, just as a sell-stop does on a stock you own. On a short that goes wrong, the worst case is roughly a 10 to 15 percent loss.

q: About shorting: a stock with a very high P/E has more than doubled and still sits above its rising 30-week average. A good short?
why: Overvaluation and 'it has run too far' are classic shorting traps. Such stocks can keep climbing for months. A short only makes sense after the stock tops out and breaks below its average into Stage 4.

q: You bought at $40, then more at $30, bringing your average cost to $35. Was buying more on the way down a smart move?
why: That is averaging down: adding money to a position that is already proving you wrong. It can leave your account weighed down by a few big losers. Add to winners, not losers.

q: Is a stock priced at $10 or less a better deal because your money buys more shares?
why: Think in dollars, not share count. Most cheap stocks are cheap for a reason, attract little institutional buying, carry wider spreads and can fall faster. Fewer shares of a quality company usually beat many cheap ones.

q: You sold a stock at a loss. It recovers and climbs above your sale price. Can buying it back higher be the right move?
why: Yes. Selling is sometimes a mistake, and fixing it means paying more. A small real account did exactly this and made a large gain, while most investors can't bring themselves to buy back higher.

q: A small account made about 40 trades, and half of them lost money. Could that account still grow strongly?
why: Yes. In a real small account, about half the trades were losers, but losses averaged about 7 % while gains averaged about 20 %. Keeping losses small let the winners carry the results.

q: A small account grew from $850 to over $51,000 in 25 years. Did it gain every single year along the way?
why: No. It made no progress in the bad market year of 1962 and had losing years in 1969 and 1974. Big long-term results still include flat and losing stretches.

q: You bought a stock at $77 and sold near $98. Would holding on for many more years have worked out better?
why: No. That stock later fell below $2. Most stocks, even great ones, eventually have to be sold, and many big winners of one era later collapse.

q: An old chart of a past winner marks its buy point at $14. Is that what buyers actually paid at the time?
why: Not necessarily. Charts of past winners are adjusted for stock splits. In one example a $14 buy point was really about $70 back then, because the stock later split 5-for-1.

q: The market is in a correction. Is that a good time to stop looking for new leading stocks?
why: No. About 90 % of cup-with-handle bases form during market corrections. The next leaders build their bases while the market falls, so keep watching.

q: Just before their big runs, did the greatest winners' charts mostly show a handful of repeating base shapes?
why: Yes. The models fall into five shapes: cup with handle, cup without handle, double bottom, flat base, and a base on top of a base. The same pictures repeat across decades.

q: Your stock breaks out, then dips back to around your buy point. Does that mean the breakout has failed?
why: Not by itself. About half the time, a breakout from a proper base pulls back to the buy point or slightly under it. It rarely drops 8 % below the exact buy point.

q: Can a daily chart reveal unusual trading on a single day that you might miss on a weekly chart?
why: Some unusual trading happens on only one day. Using a daily chart alongside the weekly one lets you catch those single-day events, such as a sudden burst of buying.

q: In a base, weeks of rising prices on heavy volume alternate with weeks of very low volume. Is that a constructive sign?
why: Heavy volume on up weeks points to big buyers stepping in. Very quiet weeks suggest the selling is exhausted. The book calls this mix of heavy up weeks and dry-ups a constructive sign.

q: While basing, a stock had six up weeks on above-average volume and two down weeks on above-average volume. Is that a good sign?
why: When up weeks on heavy volume outnumber down weeks on heavy volume while the stock is still in its base, it usually signals buying rather than selling. That tilt is generally constructive.

q: Do most bases form while the overall market is going through a correction?
why: A base is a pause after an earlier price rise, and 80 % to 90 % of them form because the general market is correcting. Market pullbacks are when the next setups get built.

q: A stock rose from $25 to $40, fell to $30, and is now back near $38. Could earlier buyers slow its climb?
why: Many who bought in the high $30s or at $40 sat on losses. As the price returns there, some sell just to break even. This selling, called overhead supply, can hold the stock back.

q: A company shows strong earnings and sales growth. Is that enough reason to buy without checking its chart?
why: Good numbers don't tell you whether the timing is right. The chart shows whether the stock is in a proper buy position or stretched too far above its base and should wait.

q: A base swung widely from high to low every week, then broke out and gained 10 %. Does that gain prove the base was sound?
why: Bases with wide weekly spreads often fail. They can still run up 5 % to 15 %, drawing in less careful traders, before breaking down badly. Tight weeks with closes near each other are what you want.

q: A stock nears a price zone where buyers got stuck three years ago. Is that resistance usually as heavy as recent resistance?
why: Overhead supply fades with time. Price areas more than two years old create less resistance, so the bigger worry is buyers trapped at recent highs.

q: Are charts mainly a buying tool, with little to say about when to sell?
why: Charts help you choose and time your buys, but they also warn you when a stock stops acting right. Spotting that change can tell you it's time to sell.

q: Can you judge a breakout well by looking at price alone and ignoring volume?
why: Volume is your best gauge of supply and demand and of big-investor buying. It shows whether a stock is being bought up or sold off, and heavy volume at key points is essential.

q: Among past top winners whose latest quarter was weak before their run, did strong profit growth usually show up the very next quarter?
why: Yes. In a study of 600 top stocks, those without big current-quarter gains made up for it in the following quarter, with an average earnings increase of 90 %.

q: A company's net income rose 12 %. Can you assume its earnings per share rose about 12 % too?
why: No. If the company issued more shares, the profit is split more ways. Net income can rise 12 % while earnings per share rise only 5 % or 6 %. Focus on per-share numbers.

q: To judge a company's December-quarter earnings, should you compare them with the September quarter just before?
why: No. Compare with the same quarter a year earlier. Many businesses are seasonal, so quarter-to-quarter comparisons can mislead. December should be measured against last year's December.

q: Quarterly profit jumped mainly because the company sold a building. Should that jump count as earnings growth?
why: No. A one-time gain like selling property says nothing about the ongoing business. Subtract it and judge growth on what operations actually earned.

q: A company growing profits about 15 % a year suddenly posts gains of 40 % to 50 %. Is that speed-up a good sign?
why: Yes. Big winners almost always showed accelerating earnings in the 10 quarters before their moves. It's not just the size of the gain, but the improvement over the old growth rate.

q: Quarterly profit growth drops from 50 % to 15 %, two quarters in a row. Is that a real warning sign?
why: Yes. Any company can have one slow quarter, but two straight quarters with growth down by two-thirds or more is a meaningful slowdown.

q: Do only about 2 % of all listed stocks show earnings gains as large as those of past top winners?
why: Yes. Only around 2 % of stocks show gains of that size. That's the point: you're hunting for rare, exceptional companies, not average ones.

q: When the late-1990s internet boom turned into a downturn, did companies with no earnings tend to fall the hardest?
why: Yes. Speculative companies with no profits suffered the biggest declines when the market corrected. Companies that actually showed earnings were the real leaders of that period.

q: Earnings went $4, $5, $6, then fell to $3. Now they're $4, up 33 %. Is that a strong report?
why: No. The 33 % looks good only because last year was so weak. Profits are still well below the $6 peak, so it's a slow recovery, not strong growth.

q: Between 1980 and 2000, was the typical yearly earnings growth of top winners, early in their runs, above 30 %?
why: Yes. The median annual growth rate was 36 % at their early emerging stage. Look for annual growth of 25 % to 50 % or more.

q: Past years show flat earnings, but analysts forecast big growth ahead. Should the forecast count as much as reported results?
why: No. Estimates are opinions and can be wrong in either direction. Reported earnings are facts. Insist on a proven record of growth, not promises.

q: On a log-scale chart, should a quality grower's quarterly earnings over several years form a nearly straight rising line?
why: Yes. Steady growers show a smooth, consistent rise in earnings, often speeding up in recent quarters. Erratic earnings point to a more cyclical, less dependable business.

q: Were about one in four past big winners cyclical or turnaround companies rather than steady growth stocks?
why: Yes. Three of four were growth stocks, but one in four was a cyclical or turnaround situation. Growth stocks remain the main hunting ground.

q: A new bull market begins. Do steel, chemical and paper stocks usually lead its early phase?
why: No. Growth stocks are usually the first to lead and make new highs. Cyclical basic-industry stocks like steel, chemicals and paper tend to lag early in a new bull market.

q: For a turnaround company, do you want two straight quarters of sharp profit recovery, lifting 12-month earnings near a new high?
why: Yes. A turnaround needs proof: two strong quarters in a row that push trailing 12-month earnings into or near new high ground. The steeper the earnings upswing, the better.

q: Does requiring three straight years of earnings growth eliminate most stocks in a typical industry group?
why: Yes. That one test weeds out about 80 % of the stocks in any group, because growth for most companies is weak or missing.

q: A company grew earnings 30 % a year for three years, but recent quarters slowed to 10 %. Is it still a prime growth stock?
why: No. When growth slows to 10 % or 15 % after a strong record, the stock tends to act like a mature company. You need both a solid record and strong recent quarters.

q: A stock has traded between $40 and $50 for months. To reach $100, must it make new price highs along the way?
why: Yes. To double from $50, it has to pass $51, $52, $53 and so on, each one a new high. Refusing to buy at new highs means refusing the path every big gain takes.

q: A stock just hit a new all-time high. Is that by itself the signal to buy?
why: No. A new high helps, but the right moment is when the stock breaks out of a proper base, ideally in a bull market. Check the chart pattern, not just the price.

q: Can a sound base, the resting period before a breakout, take more than a year to form?
why: Yes. A proper consolidation can last from about seven or eight weeks up to 15 months. Patience matters while a base forms.

q: A huge, old company launches a hot new product. Will it usually lift the stock as much as it would for a small company?
why: No. In a giant company, one new product is a small slice of total sales and earnings. That's one reason most innovation-driven winners are younger, smaller companies.

q: Can a change in top management be the new element that sparks a big stock advance?
why: Yes. New leadership that brings fresh energy and ideas is one of the triggers found behind great winners, alongside new products and changed industry conditions.

q: Can a supply shortage or rising prices across an industry be the new element that lifts its stocks?
why: Yes. New industry conditions, such as shortages, price increases or a breakthrough technology, count as something new. They can boost most stocks in a group at once.

q: A company has one hit product selling strongly. Can it coast for many years without launching anything new?
why: Unlikely. Things change fast, and a hot product's sales tend to slip within two or three years unless the company keeps bringing better new products to market.

q: Is the 'number one' company in an industry simply the biggest one or the best-known brand?
why: No. Number one means the strongest numbers: fastest earnings growth, highest return on equity, widest margins, strongest sales growth and best stock action. Size and fame don't decide it.

q: An industry group is hot. Will most stocks in it rise about as much as its top two or three?
why: No. The top one to three stocks in a strong group can soar while the rest barely move. In one tech boom, leaders rose five- to sevenfold while older giants sat still.

q: Your stock's Leadership Rank is 60, beating 60 % of stocks last year. If it rises, will it likely gain less than leaders?
why: Yes. A stock ranking below about 70 is lagging the better performers. It can still go up, but probably by less. The best picks usually rank 80 or higher.

q: Your stock's price looks fine, but its relative strength line has sunk for eight straight months. Is that a concern?
why: Yes. A relative strength line falling for seven months or more, or dropping sharply for four months or more, makes the stock's behavior questionable, and it should probably be sold.

q: When a market decline ends, are the first stocks to bounce back to new highs usually the real leaders?
why: Yes. The first stocks to reach new highs after a decline are almost always the true leaders. Breakouts keep coming for about 13 weeks, with the best often in the first three or four.

q: A former superstar drops from $82 to $50 within months. Is the big drop a bargain chance to buy?
why: No. Buying former leaders after unusually large drops has burned many professionals. One past superstar that fell from 82 to 50 kept falling to 8 and never got back to 50.

q: The market falls sharply, but one stock climbs on heavy volume. Is that strength worth noticing?
why: Yes. Strength on a weak market day is abnormal and can reveal a future leader. Several big winners showed it by rising or breaking out while the market sold off.

q: You own two stocks, one up and one down. Is selling the winner first to lock in profit usually the smarter move?
why: No. Sell the weakest first while losses are small, and give the best one room to grow. Most people do the reverse, holding losers and selling winners, which leads to bigger losses.

q: All else equal, does a stock with far fewer shares outstanding usually move up more easily when buyers arrive?
why: Yes. A smaller supply of shares takes less buying to push the price up. The tradeoff: smaller stocks can also fall just as fast, so risk is higher.

q: Is it a good sign when top managers own a meaningful stake in their own company?
why: Yes. Managers who hold a real share of the stock have a personal interest in its success. Even 1 % to 3 % in a large company counts, and more in small ones.

q: Did most of the biggest winners split their stock in the year before their big price run?
why: No. Only 18 % of them did. Oversized splits add supply, and stocks often top around their second or third split.

q: A growing company keeps buying back its own shares. Can that lift its earnings per share?
why: Yes. Fewer shares means the same profit is divided among fewer pieces, so earnings per share rise. Buybacks look most useful when earnings are already growing.

q: Is heavy debt mostly harmless for a company as long as its earnings are growing right now?
why: No. High debt can crush earnings per share when interest rates rise or a severe recession hits. Lower debt is usually safer, and a company cutting its debt is worth a look.

q: An analyst publishes a glowing research report on a stock. Does that count as the big-investor buying you want to see?
why: No. Reports and newsletters may move a stock for a few days, but they lack the sustained buying power of funds and other institutions actually owning shares.

q: A stock has no institutional owners at all. Is that a hidden-gem advantage?
why: Usually not. With thousands of institutions looking, no ownership suggests the pros passed on it. Big price moves need large buying volume, so a winner should have at least several owners.

q: Is a fund's brand-new position in a stock more telling than one it has held for years?
why: Yes. A fresh position taken in the latest quarter is more relevant. When a fund starts buying, it often keeps adding and is less likely to sell soon.

q: Fund holdings are reported about six weeks after the quarter ends. Is that too late to be useful?
why: No. Many investors think so, but these reports still help those who can spot the smarter buyers and time their entries with charts.

q: Besides pushing prices up, does institutional ownership help you find a buyer when you want to sell?
why: Yes. Fund ownership provides steady liquidity. Without it, selling in a poor market can be hard, much like trying to sell a house when buyers are scarce.

q: A whole sector is hot. Do its oldest, best-known industry groups usually lead the move?
why: No. When computers led from 1978 to 1981, the big mainframe makers lagged, while newer subgroups like minicomputers and software rose five to ten times.

q: Two key stocks in your stock's group break down hard. Should that worry you even though your stock is holding up?
why: Yes. Serious weakness in important stocks tends to spread to the rest of the group over time. Even widely praised stocks have later fallen with their weakening group.

q: Your stock looks strong, but no other important stock in its group is acting well. Is it a sound buy?
why: Usually not. A practical rule is to buy only when at least one other important stock in the same group confirms the strength. Truly unique companies are rare exceptions.

q: Can a boom in one industry later lift a related one, like more air travel boosting hotels?
why: Yes. This follow-on effect is common. Jet planes sparked an airline boom, and the extra travelers later created a hotel shortage that sent hotel stocks soaring.

q: When an industry booms, can a small supplier to it become a big winner too?
why: Yes. As airlines bought new jets, a maker of the planes' onboard toilets grew earnings 200 % and its stock rose about 1,000 %. Look at who supplies the leaders.

q: After two strong bull-market years, buying flows into utilities, food and gold stocks. Is that a bullish sign?
why: Not usually. Buying in defensive groups like gold, food, tobacco and utilities after a couple of bull years can signal that a market top is approaching.

q: Did most of the top winners from 1953 to 1993 rise on their own, without their industry group moving too?
why: No. Nearly two out of three were part of group advances. Watching which groups are moving is a key part of finding the next winners.

q: In bull markets, do the sectors with the most stocks making new highs tend to hold most of the real leaders?
why: Yes. Checking which broad sectors have the most stocks at new highs each day, and noting the top six or so, usually points you to where most true leaders are.

q: After a long rise, a stock's 200-day moving average starts to turn down. Is that a reason to consider selling?
why: A 200-day line that turns down after a prolonged upswing is listed among the signs that a stock is breaking support. It's a cue to consider selling.

q: A stock hits a new high, but most of its base sat below the 200-day moving average. Is that a good buy?
why: A base that does most of its work in its lower half or below the 200-day line is weak. New highs off such a base are listed as a time to sell, not to buy.

q: Your stock now trades about 80 % above its 200-day moving average. Could that be a sign to take profits?
why: Stocks 70 % to 100 % or more above their 200-day line after a big run can be candidates to sell. It is one of the weaker signals, so use it together with others.

q: A new leader jumped 20 % in three weeks, then dipped to its 10-week average for the first time. Must you sell?
why: Stocks that gain 20 % or more in one to four weeks are often the most powerful. The book suggests holding them through the first couple of pullbacks to, or slightly below, the 10-week line.

q: In a study across many bull markets, did stocks making new highs tend to outperform stocks making new lows?
why: The study compared stocks on the new-high list with those on the new-low list. New-high stocks tended to go higher and new-low stocks tended to go lower, the reverse of buy low, sell high.

q: In 1990, Cisco hit the highest price it had ever traded at. Would buying right then have paid off hugely?
why: It looked scary at a record price, yet buying then would have meant a gain of nearly 75,000 % by its peak in 2000. A new high can be the start of a move, not the end.

q: When a top mutual fund's new purchases were studied, had each stock been bought at its highest price of the past year?
why: Over a hundred purchases were checked, and every one was made at the highest price of the prior year, as the stock broke into new highs from a chart pattern.

q: In 2008 a leading oil stock closed below its 10-week average every week, yet analysts called it a bargain. A buy?
why: Closing under the 10-week line week after week marked a slow topping process. Institutions that bought because it looked cheap were too early, as oil kept collapsing.

q: Can a proper cup-with-handle pattern take longer than a year to form?
why: Cups can last from 7 weeks up to 65 weeks, though most take three to six months. A long base isn't ruled out just by its length.

q: A cup fell about 30 % from its peak to its low. Is that too deep to count as a normal cup?
why: The usual cup corrects from around 12 % to 15 % up to about 33 % from peak to low. A 30 % drop sits inside that range.

q: Before forming its cup, a stock rose only 10 %. Does that meet the prior uptrend you want to see?
why: A strong base should follow a clear uptrend of at least 30 %, ideally with improving relative strength and some bursts of heavy volume along the way.

q: Is a sharp V-shaped cup bottom generally better than a rounded U-shaped one?
why: A rounded U gives the stock time to correct and shake out weak holders with a few final dips. That leaves stronger owners, who are less likely to sell in the next advance.

q: The market corrects 10 % and a growth stock's base falls 22 %. Is that still within a normal range?
why: Growth stocks usually fall 1½ to 2½ times as much as the market in a correction. A 22 % drop is 2.2 times the market. Declines beyond 2½ times deserve suspicion.

q: A stock fell 55 % from its peak while basing. Must it more than double just to get back to its old high?
why: After a fall of over 50 %, a stock needs a gain of more than 100 % to regain its high. Such patterns fail more often, and new highs from them tend to break down 5 % to 15 % past the breakout.

q: Can a stock that fell about 50 % while building its base still become a huge winner?
why: It's rare, but it happens. One stock fell about 50 % in a 1975 market decline, formed a well-shaped cup with handle, then rose 554 %. How deep a base gets depends partly on how hard the market fell.

q: In a bull market, a handle pulls back 18 % from its peak. Is that a normal handle?
why: In bull markets, a proper handle's dip should stay within 8 % to 12 % of its peak, unless the cup is very large. Deeper handles look wide and erratic and are usually risky.

q: Near a bear market bottom, a handle drops 25 %. Can the pattern still be sound?
why: In the last shakeout of a bear market, some handles fall 20 % to 30 %. The pattern can still work if the market then follows through and starts a new major uptrend.

q: A cup forms with no handle at all. Is it doomed to fail?
why: Cups without handles fail somewhat more often, but many stocks advance successfully without one. Some fast-moving leaders formed handles of just one or two weeks before big runs.

q: A handle sits in the upper half of the base but below the 10-week moving average. Is that a strong handle?
why: A handle should form in the upper half of the base and also above the 10-week line. Handles completely below that line are described as weak and failure-prone.

q: In a W-shaped double bottom, the second low dips slightly below the first. Is that a warning sign?
why: Undercutting the first low is normal and useful: it shakes out weaker holders. A second low that fails to undercut can create a weaker, more failure-prone pattern.

q: A stock rose 25 % off a cup with handle, then moved sideways for seven weeks, dipping only 12 %. Is that a flat base?
why: A flat base usually follows a gain of 20 % or more off an earlier base. It moves sideways in a fairly tight range for at least five or six weeks and corrects no more than 10 % to 15 %.

q: You missed a stock's breakout from a cup with handle. Could it still give you another chance to buy later?
why: Keep it on your watch list. After its first move, a stock may build a flat base, which can offer a second opportunity to get on board.

q: A stock doubled in six weeks, then drifted sideways for three weeks, slipping 15 %. Could this be the strongest pattern of all?
why: That fits a high, tight flag: a 100 % to 120 % run in four to eight weeks, then a sideways rest of 10 % to 25 %. It's the strongest pattern, but rare, risky and hard to read.

q: In a late bear market, a stock breaks out, stalls, and builds a second base on top of the first. Could that signal strength?
why: When the market keeps falling, a strong stock can't make its normal 20 % to 30 % gain and bases again right on top of the old base. Once the decline ends, such stocks are often among the first to new highs.

q: A stock pulls back three times, 10 % to 20 % each, with every low below the one before. Is that an ascending base?
why: An ascending base also has three pullbacks of 10 % to 20 %, but each low is higher than the previous one. Lower lows don't fit the pattern.

q: A stock pauses sideways for just two weeks after a run. Is that a reliable base to buy from?
why: Apart from a few special cases, reliable bases need at least seven to eight weeks of consolidation. Bases of one, two or three weeks are risky and should almost always be avoided.

q: A stock's base looked wide and loose, so you crossed it off. Should it stay off your list for good?
why: Wide, loose patterns usually fail, but some later tighten into sound bases and go on to big gains. Clinging to an old opinion of a stock can make you miss the moment it changes.

q: Your stock breaks out of its fourth base since its run began. Could such late bases fail as often as 80 % of the time?
why: By the third or fourth base, the stock is obvious to everyone and patterns turn wider and looser. As many as 80 % of fourth-stage bases should fail, if you count the stage correctly.

q: A stock rose 12 % over the past three months and is now resting sideways. Does that rise meet the size this setup looks for?
why: No. The setup starts with a big move higher in the past one to three months, roughly 30 % to 100 % or more. A 12 % rise is too small to show real force behind the stock.

q: A stock ran up 60 % and has paused for only three days. Has it already formed the kind of rest this setup typically needs?
why: Not yet. The resting phase usually lasts about two weeks to two months, with higher lows and a tightening range. Three days is far short of that.

q: Looking at a century of big winning stocks, do leaders tend to climb in steps: a big move, a sideways pause, then another move?
why: Yes. Leading stocks rarely rise in a straight line. They tend to jump 20 % to 50 % or more, pull back and drift sideways, then move again. That repeating pause is what this setup trades.

q: Does this tight setup after a big move only work on the daily chart, not on weekly or intraday charts?
why: No. On the daily chart it is a swing-trading setup, but the same pattern also shows up on weekly charts and on 1- and 5-minute charts.

q: For the very strongest stocks, is the 10-day average the best place to find support during the rest, ahead of the 20- and 50-day?
why: Yes. The strongest names tend to hold the 10-day, strong ones the 20-day, and slower ones the 50-day. A setup can form at any of them, but the 10-day is the best.

q: The index is falling, but a stock holds steady or drifts sideways. Is that a point in its favour as a candidate?
why: Yes. A stock that refuses to drop while the market sells off is showing strength against the market. That is one of the traits to look for before the setup forms.

q: A stock gaps up 6 % on strong earnings. Is that gap big enough to count as a news-driven pivot?
why: No. A news-driven pivot needs a gap of at least 10 %, together with heavy volume. A 6 % gap can still be a fine move, but it does not meet this setup's bar.

q: Great earnings, a big beat on estimates, and a gap up. But the stock sells off all day. Is it still a news-driven pivot?
why: No. Strong numbers alone are not enough. The source shows a case with big earnings and a big beat where the stock gapped only slightly and sold off, and says plainly it was not this setup.

q: On a big news gap, is it a good sign if the stock trades its normal daily volume within the first 15 to 30 minutes?
why: Yes. Heavy volume early is what you want. Many of the best examples traded a full day's average volume within the first 15 to 30 minutes after the open.

q: A stock already rallied for several months before gapping up on earnings. Does that earlier run make the gap a stronger setup?
why: No. It works best when the stock has not rallied in the prior three to six months. If it already climbed for months, the good news may not be much of a surprise to the market.

q: Can unexpected good news on a neglected, overlooked stock set off a move that lasts months or even years?
why: Yes. Surprise is the fuel. When good news hits a stock few people are watching, it can start a long move. Earnings and guidance surprises are the main type to look for.

q: A small company gaps up on earnings but has no analysts covering it. Can it still qualify, judged on its growth numbers and volume?
why: Yes. Many smaller stocks have no analyst coverage, so there is no estimate to beat. In that case you rely on the growth figures themselves and on the heavy volume.

q: Can a new leader's breakout volume run 500 % or more above its daily average?
why: Look for at least 40 % to 50 % above normal, but new leaders often show spikes of 200 %, 500 % or even 1,000 %. Microsoft broke out on volume 545 % above average.

q: In a cup with handle, should you wait until price clears the base's highest point before buying?
why: Most buy points sit 5 % to 10 % below the prior peak and are set by the high of the handle. Waiting for a true new high often means buying too late.

q: Can a downtrend line drawn across a base's peaks sometimes give you an earlier entry than the handle's high?
why: Draw a line from the base's highest point down across the peak where the handle begins. A break above it can give a slight head start, but only if your chart reading is right.

q: To get a better price, you buy a few percent before the stock reaches its pivot. Is that a smart edge?
why: Buying early is premature. In many cases the stock never reaches its breakout point and stalls or falls instead. Let it prove its strength by trading at the buy point first.

q: You bought right at a correct pivot, and the stock is now up 2 %. Is adding more shares a sound move?
why: Adding as a stock rises, called averaging up, fits when the first buy was made at a correct pivot and the price has gained 2 % or 3 %. You follow up on what is working.

q: When you add to a winning position, should each new purchase be bigger than the one before?
why: The method follows up on what is working, but each additional purchase is smaller than the first. Most people do the reverse and add to stocks that are falling.

q: After a correct breakout, do most big winners close below their pivot point at some stage?
why: Winning stocks very rarely fall 8 % below a correct pivot, and most big winners don't close below it at all. Buying close to the pivot lets you spot trouble early.

q: After a sound breakout, your stock slips back to your exact buy point. Can a true winner do that?
why: Between 40 % and 60 % of the time, a winning stock pulls back to its buy point or slightly below, as if to shake you out. It shouldn't fall 8 % unless you bought too high.

q: During a bear market, a stock breaks out of a good-looking base. Should you buy the breakout?
why: In bear markets most breakouts fail. The bases tend to be too deep, wide or loose, often late-stage or with handles in the lower half. The method still works; the timing is wrong.

q: A stock pushes through a price zone where earlier buyers were stuck. Could it be safer to buy now, despite the higher price?
why: Fighting through overhead supply shows there's enough demand to absorb those sellers. A stock breaking into new high ground for the first time has no such supply to deal with.

q: Can you enter a breakout from the daily chart alone, buying as the stock starts to break out, without any intraday chart?
why: Yes. Intraday opening-range highs are one way in, but they are optional. Watching the daily chart and entering as the stock begins to break out also works.

q: Is buying before the breakout, in anticipation of it, the more effective way to trade this setup?
why: No. Buying early can work, but it is less effective and takes more skill and experience. Waiting for the stock to actually break out is the main approach.

q: Today's low is $100 and the stock's ATR is $30. It's now trading at $135. Is it still a valid entry?
why: No. If the price has already risen more than one ATR above the day's low, you skip it. Here the limit is $130, so at $135 the day has run too far.

q: A stock is breaking out, but earnings come out in two days. Is skipping the buy in line with the method?
why: Yes. The rule is not to buy in the three days before a quarterly report.

q: Do most breakouts in this approach happen within the first 30 minutes of the trading day?
why: Yes. Most breakouts come early, in the first half hour.

q: The index slips about 10 % during the first year of a bull market. Can the bull market still be intact?
why: Early bull markets usually include a few pullbacks lasting a couple of months, typically 8 % to 12 % and now and then up to 15 %. A dip of that size alone does not end the uptrend.

q: After a bear market, is it smart to wait until the economy clearly improves before you start buying stocks again?
why: Stocks look months ahead, so bear markets usually end while business news is still getting worse. Waiting for the economy to recover means buying well after the market has already turned up.

q: The index falls 3 % in the morning but closes higher for the day. Can that count as day one of a rally attempt?
why: A rally attempt starts on the first day an index closes higher after a decline, even if the drop happened earlier the same session. Counting from that day tells you when to start watching for a follow-through.

q: On day five of a rally attempt, the index jumps 2 %, but volume is lower than the day before. Is that a follow-through day?
why: A follow-through needs a strong gain on volume higher than the previous session, and ideally above average. A big price jump on lighter volume lacks the proof that large buyers are returning.

q: A follow-through day just confirmed a new uptrend. Should you put all your cash to work right away?
why: The signal only gives a green light to start buying top-quality stocks as they break out of sound bases. You build positions as those setups appear, not by buying everything at once.

q: Has a new bull market ever started without a strong follow-through day on rising price and volume?
why: In the record studied, every new bull market began with a powerful price and volume follow-through. That is why it pays to wait for one instead of guessing the bottom.

q: After a long rally, cheap low-quality stocks start leading the most-active list on up days. Is that a healthy sign for the market?
why: When the original leaders falter and weaker, speculative names take over, the advance is running on its last legs. Laggards cannot carry a market higher for long.

q: The index closes down 0.1 % on higher volume than the day before. Does that count as a distribution day?
why: A down day on higher volume counts only if the index loses more than 0.2 %. A tiny dip like 0.1 % is too small to show real selling by big investors.

q: After the first drop from a top, the index bounces but regains less than half the loss. Reason for more caution?
why: A feeble bounce, one that recovers under half the drop, gains little, or rises on shrinking volume, often fails. Seeing it after a top is a signal to sell more, not to buy.

q: Have three big interest-rate hikes in a row by the central bank often marked the start of bear markets?
why: Historically, three successive significant Fed rate increases have generally come at the beginning of bear markets and recessions. Still, the market's own price and volume action remains the main gauge.

q: Bad news hits the headlines, but the market barely reacts. Can that actually be a positive sign?
why: How the market responds matters more than whether news sounds good or bad. Shrugging off bad news suggests the market is stronger underneath than most people think.

q: During a bear market, can a convincing rally last for months and still turn out to be a fake?
why: Bear markets usually fall in several legs, interrupted by rallies that last just long enough to lure buyers back. In 1969 and 1974 some of these false rallies ran up to 15 weeks.

q: In the 1973-74 bear market, the Dow fell 50 %. Did the average stock hold up better than that?
why: The average stock did far worse, falling more than 70 %. Popular indexes can understate how much damage a bear market does to typical stocks.

q: The index makes new highs while the advance-decline line lags, but only for a few weeks. Is a mere correction the likely result?
why: A short gap between the index and breadth usually points to a correction inside an ongoing bull market. The longer the gap lasts, over several months, the more serious the trouble.

q: A 200-day average of daily advances minus declines drops from positive to below zero. Is that a bearish signal?
why: This breadth momentum gauge gives its key signal when it crosses zero. A move from positive to negative warns that the long-term trend is weakening; the reverse is favourable.

q: Does the 200-day breadth momentum gauge give its earliest warnings at market bottoms rather than at tops?
why: It works the other way. Its sell signals tend to come early at tops, while at bottoms it is somewhat late and mainly confirms a new rally is real.

q: The breadth momentum gauge hovered near zero, then pops just above it. Is that as strong as a cross after months deep below zero?
why: A cross means more the longer the gauge has stayed on one side and the deeper it went. Flicking across zero from a hover is far less meaningful.

q: The index keeps falling, but weekly new highs minus new lows has begun trending higher. Could that be an early bullish sign?
why: It shows fewer stocks are following the index down, a sign of strength building beneath the surface. A positive split like this helped flag the start of a major bull market in 1982.

q: Are the biggest moves in the U.S. market most likely when most foreign stock markets point the same way?
why: Markets around the world are tied together. The most profitable U.S. moves, up or down, tend to come when the large majority of world markets agree.

q: After a brutal bear market, a major magazine puts a terrifying bear on its cover. Is that a reason to sell more?
why: Extreme fear in headlines often appears near bottoms. In late 1974 such a cover came as other indicators turned positive, a time to start buying rather than sell.

q: Is it wise to rely mainly on one or two favourite indicators to judge the market's trend?
why: Any indicator, however good its record, will mislead you at some point. Reading the combined message of many gauges makes it much less likely you end up on the wrong side.

q: Only one of every three picks works, but the average gain is over twice the average loss. Can the account still end the year ahead?
why: It happened in a real account during a year the market dropped 29 %. Keeping losses small while letting winners grow means you can be wrong most of the time and still profit.

q: If you buy stocks during a bear market, should you give them more room than the usual 7-8 % before selling?
why: Bear markets call for less room, not more. If you buy at all in a weak market, cut losses much sooner, around 3 % to 4 %, because breakouts fail more often.

q: Your stock fell from $40 to $28, but you haven't sold. Have you already taken a real loss?
why: Your shares are worth $28 now whether you sell or not. Selling doesn't create the loss; it only admits it and frees the money for a better choice.

q: Your new stock is down just 3 %, acting poorly, and the market is under heavy selling. Must you wait for 8 %?
why: The 7-8 % figure is the maximum, not a target. If the market shows distribution or the stock starts off wrong, you can cut the loss earlier.

q: After a 33 % loss, do you need a 50 % gain just to get back to even?
why: A $10,000 account that drops to about $6,667 must gain roughly $3,333, which is 50 %, to recover. The deeper the loss, the faster the gain needed to repair it grows.

q: Your stock slipped past your sell point and is now down 12 %. Is it too late to sell?
why: A stock that falls further and faster than normal is in more trouble, which makes selling even more urgent. Waiting risks turning a 12 % loss into a much bigger one.

q: You need cash. Should you sell your weakest performer first, even if it's the one showing a loss?
why: What you paid has no effect on what a stock will do next. Selling the laggard and keeping the stronger stock removes the weed, not the flower.

q: A stock is down 35 %, but it pays a 4 % dividend. Does the dividend make the position roughly okay?
why: A 35 % price loss plus 4 % income still leaves a 31 % net loss. Dividends are not a reason to sit with a stock that is falling.

q: In a severe bear market, does owning 20 or 30 different stocks protect you from big losses?
why: In a bad bear market almost all stocks fall, and some never recover. Owning many stocks can also slow you down when it is time to sell and raise cash.

q: With a fully margined account, do you lose your own money about twice as fast when your stocks fall?
why: With half the money borrowed, every drop in your stocks hits your own capital twice as hard. A 50 % fall in risky stocks could wipe the account out.

q: Your broker issues a margin call after a stock drops. Is adding more money usually the better choice than selling?
why: A margin call means the market is telling you something is wrong. Selling stock and cutting risk works out better most of the time than putting more money into a falling position.

q: If you buy right at a breakout from a sound base, should an 8 % drop below your price be fairly rare?
why: Well-timed buys from sound bases seldom fall 8 %. When one does, either the pick was a mistake or the whole market may be starting to decline.

q: You cut a loss at 7 %, and the stock then rebounds. Can selling still have been the right decision?
why: Cutting losses works like insurance: you pay a small premium to avoid a disaster. A rebound later doesn't mean the protection was wasted, just as an unused car policy isn't.

q: You buy a stock that gapped up 15 % on news. Should your stop sit below where the price was before the gap?
why: No. The stop goes at the low of the day you buy, not below the old pre-gap price.

q: With a $10,000 account, is risking $300 on a single trade within the usual 0.25–1 % risk per trade?
why: No. $300 is 3 % of the account. The usual risk per trade is 0.25 % to 1 %, and rarely more than 1 %.

q: Is it acceptable to hold a larger slice of your account in one stock during the day than overnight?
why: Yes. The cap for one stock held overnight is 30 % of the account. During the day you can go bigger, because there is no overnight gap that could jump past your stop.

q: Should a stop-loss be placed as a limit order rather than a market order?
why: No. Use market stops, not limit stops. A limit stop may never fill in a fast drop, and then the loss keeps growing.

q: A stock averages 1 million shares a day. Could you buy 50,000 shares and stay within the sizing rule?
why: No. The rule caps a position at 1 % of the stock's average volume. With 1 million shares a day, that is at most 10,000 shares.

q: Can a trader be very profitable while winning only about 25 % to 30 % of trades?
why: Yes. The edge comes from keeping losses small and letting winners grow to many times the risk. With that, a 25 % to 30 % win rate can be very profitable.

q: Is the best time to sell a winning stock usually while it's still rising and looks strong to everyone?
why: Selling into strength lets you lock in gains before the 20 % to 40 % pullbacks that can hit leaders. You won't catch the exact top, and that's fine.

q: You bought at $50, it reached $60, and now it's back at $52. Is it reasonable to let it fall below $50?
why: Missing the profit at $60 was one mistake. Letting a stock that rose close to 20 % turn into a loss would be a second, avoidable mistake.

q: As a stock climbs, should you keep moving a tight stop-loss just below the current price?
why: Stocks need room for normal pullbacks. A stop trailed too closely will likely sell you near the low of an ordinary correction instead of near a real top.

q: After a breakout from a proper base, do most winners pull back at some point between the second and sixth week?
why: About 80 % of the time a stock dips somewhere in weeks two to six after breaking out. Holding through the first eight weeks helps you sit through that first shakeout.

q: If you make two separate 20 % gains in one year, does that compound to about 44 %?
why: Gaining 20 % and then another 20 % on the larger sum gives 1.2 times 1.2, or 1.44. Quick 20 % gains, reinvested, add up fast.

q: When adding to a winning stock, should each follow-up purchase be larger than your first one?
why: Follow-up buys should be smaller than the first. That way you add to what is working without pushing your average cost up too much.

q: If you buy stocks during a bear market, should you hold out for the usual 20-25 % profit target?
why: In a bear market gains are smaller and less reliable. If you buy at all, take profits around 15 % and cut losses at about 3 %.

q: Quarterly earnings growth slows from 60 % to 20 % for two quarters in a row. Should you consider selling?
why: A sharp slowdown, about two-thirds below the earlier growth rate, for two straight quarters is a common reason to sell. The story that drove the stock is losing steam.

q: A scary rumor about your stock spreads online. Should you sell the moment you hear it?
why: Bad news and rumors often have only a short-lived effect, and some are spread to scare small investors out. Base the decision on how the stock actually trades.

q: Do most investors tend to cash in profits quickly while holding on to their losers?
why: Emotion pushes people to grab small gains and wait on losses. The better habit is the reverse: cut losses quickly and let profits develop slowly.

q: A thinly owned stock with no strength in its industry jumps 20 % in three weeks. Must you hold it for eight weeks?
why: The eight-week hold is for strong leaders. Poorer-quality stocks without big-fund ownership or a strong group behind them don't earn that extra patience.

q: Can you pick the right stocks at the right time for a full year and still end up only breaking even?
why: It happened in a real account in 1961. The buys were right, but with no plan for taking profits, the gains vanished when the stocks topped.

q: You're new to trading the rest of a winning position. Should you trail it with the 20-day average rather than the 10-day?
why: No. Beginners are told to stick to the 10-day average and to exit on the first close below it. The 20-day is an option for slower stocks once you have more experience.

q: Mid-session, your stock dips just below its 10-day average. Should you sell the rest right away, before the close?
why: No. The signal is a close below the 10-day, not a dip during the day.

q: In a strong market, is it common for well-chosen breakouts to gain 10 to 20 times the initial risk or more?
why: Yes. With good setup selection in a bullish market, moves of 10 to 20 times the initial risk or more are common.

q: Is the 10-day average better suited for trailing a fast-moving stock, and the 20-day for a calmer one?
why: Yes. Which average to trail depends on how fast the stock moves. Fast movers get the tighter 10-day, while slower ones get room on the 20-day.

q: Your stock falls below one of its recent higher lows. Is that a reason to sell under this method?
why: Yes. Rising lows show buyers stepping in higher each time. When one of them breaks, that structure is gone, and the method says to sell.

q: You have a large gain when a big market decline begins. Is riding it out with your old leader the suggested approach?
why: No. Even a big gain is not a reason to sit through a large decline. The advice is to step aside and buy the new leaders that emerge afterwards.

q: After months of gains, a stock rises on 8 of 10 days with its widest weekly range of the run. Is that a sell signal?
why: This is a climax top: a sudden, faster run after a long advance. The week's high-to-low range is usually the largest since the move began, and the end is often close.

q: A stock gaps up two weeks after breaking out of its first base. Is that the classic exhaustion gap that signals a top?
why: An exhaustion gap comes after a long run, usually at least 18 weeks out of a first- or second-stage base. A gap early in a move can simply show strong demand.

q: Near the end of a fast run, a week has huge volume but the stock barely closes higher. Is that a warning sign?
why: Heavy volume with little price progress means big holders are selling into the buying. On a weekly chart this can look like two parallel bars, a sign of distribution.

q: An already extended stock jumps 30 % in two weeks after announcing a stock split. Is that a reason to hold for more?
why: A 25 % to 50 % surge in a week or two around a split is a classic topping sign. Stocks often peak around excessive splits, so selling is usually the better move.

q: After a stock peaks, do runs of down days tend to get longer than the runs of up days?
why: In an uptrend you might see four up days, then two or three down. After a top this often flips to four or five down days followed by only two or three up.

q: A stock keeps making new highs while its volume steadily shrinks. Does that show strong demand?
why: Rising prices on falling volume suggest big investors are losing interest. New highs without the volume behind them are a possible sign of a top.

q: Is a breakout from a fourth-stage base usually about as reliable as one from a first-stage base?
why: By the third or fourth base the stock is obvious to everyone, and those bases are often wider and looser. As many as 80 % of fourth-stage bases should fail.

q: After heavy selling near a top, the stock bounces for a couple of days on light volume. Is that bounce a good chance to sell?
why: A weak recovery after heavy selling often fails. Selling on the second or third day of a poor rally may be the last good exit before support breaks.

q: Your stock hits new highs, but no other important stock in its industry is showing strength. Is that reassuring?
why: A lone winner without support from its group is a warning. Real leadership usually comes with other strong stocks in the same industry.

q: After a long advance, a stock closes below its 10-week average and stays under it for eight or nine weeks. Is that a sell signal?
why: A healthy leader quickly climbs back above its 10-week line. Weeks of failing to close above it show that the uptrend has broken down.

q: Your extended stock lands on a major magazine cover and everyone is excited. Is that a good reason to hold with more confidence?
why: Big investors need eager buyers to sell to, and wide publicity brings those buyers in. When everyone is already optimistic and fully invested, little buying power is left.

q: Can a leading stock top out while its quarterly earnings are still up more than 100 %?
why: Many leaders peak while earnings look excellent. In 2008 a fertilizer leader topped with its quarter up 181 %, fooling analysts who watched only the earnings.

q: A stock has based for months, yet volume starts rising while the price barely moves. Is that a favourable sign?
why: It suggests disappointed owners are no longer pushing the price down, and buyers are taking their shares without demanding a lower price. Demand is quietly building.

q: At the ideal moment a stock breaks out into Stage 2, do its reported fundamentals often still look poor?
why: The chart often turns before the news does. At the perfect buy point the reported numbers can look negative, and a broker may even try to talk you out of buying.

q: Your stock starts forming a Stage 3 top after a big run. As a long-term investor, should you sell every share right away?
why: The suggested move is to take profits on half. The stock could still break out into a new advance. Protect the other half with a sell stop just below the top's support.

q: A stock with a P/E of 10 and rising earnings breaks below Stage 3 support. Does the low P/E make it safe to hold?
why: The chart showed trouble despite the cheap valuation. In one such case the stock fell more than 50 % over the next six months, during a great bull market.

q: After a stock breaks down into Stage 4, is a rally back up toward the breakdown level common?
why: Bargain hunters often step in because the price looks cheap next to recent levels. That rally usually fails, and then the real decline gets going below a falling average.

q: The index hits a high, drops, rallies to a lower peak, then falls below the earlier dip. Is that a topping signal?
why: A lower peak followed by a break of the prior low is a classic sign of a top. In 1987 this pattern, plus a flattening 30-week average, came just before the crash.

q: In 1973 Avon was seen as a stock you never had to sell. About 14 years after its top, was it back near its high?
why: It was still far below. Its high was 140, and in late 1987 it was struggling in the mid-30s. No investment is buy-and-forget; holding through Stage 4 is costly.

q: The main index has just broken below its 30-week average into Stage 4. A few stocks still break out. Should you buy them?
why: When the market itself enters Stage 4 it is time to turn defensive. Hold off on buying even if some charts look good, and sell stocks showing weak relative strength.

q: The market average has entered Stage 4. Should you pull the stops on your remaining stocks up as tight as possible?
why: In a market breakdown you protect what you still hold. Tighter stops limit how much you give back if the decline drags your stocks down too.

q: When the market enters a high-risk zone, do false signals and whipsaws on individual stock charts become more likely?
why: Near major tops, setups that look fine fail more often. That is why it pays to build cash and be very selective about new buys in those periods.

q: Late in a bear market, indicators say risk is now low. Is it time to lock in short-sale profits and prepare for selective buying?
why: A low-risk zone at the end of a decline is the moment to stop pressing the downside. Close out shorts, build cash, and get ready to buy the best setups.

q: Do bear markets turn up so suddenly that you must buy bargains on the way down to avoid missing the rally?
why: Turns usually give plenty of warning beforehand. Signs such as a key bellwether stock forming a base let you wait for evidence instead of guessing the bottom.

q: A valuation gauge says stocks are very expensive, but the trend indicators are still bullish. Should you go fully to cash now?
why: Valuation can flag danger a year or more early. Selling stocks when they first looked overvalued in 1928 or 1986 would have missed two big rallies. Stay long with an eye on the exit.

q: Did the October 1987 crash arrive without any warning from the market's own trend signals?
why: Before the crash, the index set a lower peak, its 30-week average flattened, and it broke below that average. That was a clear Stage 4 sell signal days before the big drop.

q: For short sellers: does a typical stock fall faster than it rises?
why: Fear sparks panic selling quickly, while greed builds slowly. That speed is part of why shorting the right breakdowns can pay off fast.

q: About shorting: a stock breaks down, but the rest of its industry group is very strong. Is it a good short?
why: Shorting works best with a weak stock in a weak group in a falling market. A strong group can hold the stock up, so look elsewhere.

q: About shorting: a hyped stock has short interest about ten times its daily volume. Does that make a quick fall more likely?
why: A huge short position can push the price higher as short sellers rush to buy back on every rally. These crowded shorts often fall only after the early shorts are wiped out.

q: About shorting: as a careful investor, should you wait for a pullback to the breakdown level before shorting your whole position?
why: Pullbacks after breakdowns happen less often than after breakouts, so you may never get in. Short half on the breakdown and the other half on any pullback.

q: About shorting: a stock already down sharply moves sideways under its falling average, then breaks lower. Can it still be a good short?
why: Big losers often fall much further. After a consolidation below a declining average, a fresh breakdown can bring another fast drop, as long as a sensible buy-stop fits overhead.

q: About shorting: the buy-stop for a great-looking setup must sit 30 % to 40 % above entry. Should you pick another stock?
why: Part of choosing a good short is being able to protect it with a stop not too far away. If two shorts look equally weak, pick the one with the closer stop.

q: About shorting: in a head-and-shoulders top, the heaviest volume shows up on the right shoulder. Should you trust the pattern?
why: Heavy buying on the right shoulder means demand is still strong. That pattern is more likely to trap short sellers, so look elsewhere.

q: About shorting: does a head-and-shoulders top built over nine months usually lead to a bigger drop than one built in three weeks?
why: The longer the top takes, the more buyers get trapped at high prices. When they finally panic and sell, the fall tends to be larger.

q: When shorting stretched stocks, is the 10- and 20-day average area the usual profit target?
why: Yes. After a parabolic run, these stocks usually fall back toward their 10- and 20-day averages and bounce there. That zone is where a short is taken off.

q: About shorting: a small company's stock jumped 60 % in a week. Is that already stretched enough for a parabolic short?
why: No. For smaller companies the setup needs a far bigger run, roughly 300 % to 1000 % or more. The 50 % to 100 % range applies to larger companies.

q: When shorting a parabolic stock, is a wide, loose stop the safer choice so normal swings don't shake you out?
why: No. The key is a relatively tight, clearly defined stop: the high of the day, or a move back above VWAP if you entered on a VWAP failure.

q: About shorting: the stock cracks, bounces back up to VWAP, and fails there. Is that a valid point to enter the short?
why: Yes. A failed bounce into VWAP is one of the entries for this short, and also a place to add. The stop then goes at a reclaim of VWAP.

q: Of the three setups, is shorting parabolic stocks the riskiest if done wrong or without obeying stops?
why: Yes. Of the three setups, shorting parabolic stocks is by far the riskiest when done badly or when stops are not respected.

q: About shorting: does a parabolic short typically offer a bigger reward-to-risk than a breakout or a news gap trade?
why: No. Breakouts and news gaps can sometimes pay 30 to 50 times the risk or more. Parabolic shorts are more like 5 to 10 times, though the win rate can be higher if you wait.

q: Is the most common investor mistake simply never going back to study your own past buys and sells?
why: Most investors never review where their trades went wrong, so they keep repeating the same errors. Finding and fixing your own mistakes is the step most people skip.

q: After 20 years of investing, is your experience by itself a reliable sign you'll do better than a beginner?
why: Experience only helps if it teaches better habits. Years of repeating the same mistakes just make them stronger. What counts is avoiding the classic errors, at any level of experience.

q: In 2000, Cisco fell from $82 and people bought at $50. Did it get back to $50 in the 2003-2007 bull market?
why: It never returned to $50, even during the next bull market, and by January 2009 it traded near $16. Buying a falling stock because it looks cheap can trap money for years.

q: You have clear rules for what to buy. Is it fine to work out when to sell later, once you own it?
why: Most investors have no selling plan, which means they have done only half the work. Knowing when and why you will sell belongs to the plan before you buy.

q: Can a company that pays a large dividend actually be the weaker business?
why: Strong growers usually reinvest their cash in research and growth instead of paying it out. A company paying out a lot may be weaker, and a day or two of price swings can wipe out the dividend.

q: A friend's hot tip about a company turns out to be true. Is the stock then most likely to go up?
why: Most tips and rumors are false, and even true ones often see the stock fall instead of rise. Acting on what others say replaces your own study with hope.

q: You used to work at a big, famous company. Does knowing it well make its stock a better buy?
why: Familiarity is not a buying reason. Many of the best investments are newer companies you have never heard of, found with a little research before others notice them.

q: You sell winners fast to lock in small gains, but give losers more time to recover. Is that the right way round?
why: It is exactly backwards. The sound habit is to cut losses quickly and give your winners more time to grow.

q: Your stock is weakening, but you're a few months from a lower long-term tax rate. Is that a good reason to keep holding?
why: Making a net profit comes first. Holding on too long to get a better tax rate can throw away a good gain. Refusing to sell because of taxes is usually pride, not sound judgment.

q: Is being able to sell quickly and cheaply one of the big advantages of owning stocks over owning real estate?
why: Low trading costs and fast exits mean you can protect yourself quickly when a stock turns against you. Commissions are small next to the cost of a wrong decision.

q: Can using limit orders to save a few cents leave you stuck in a stock you really should sell?
why: Haggling over tiny price differences takes your eye off the bigger move. With a limit order you risk missing the trade entirely, including the exit that would have avoided a big loss.

q: If you often can't decide whether to buy, sell or hold, does that usually mean you lack clear rules?
why: Not knowing what to do is a symptom. It shows there is no proven plan or set of buy and sell rules to lean on when a decision is needed.

q: Does wanting to get rich fast tend to make you slow to cut your losses?
why: Chasing quick money without preparation leads people to jump into stocks too fast. The same impatience then leaves them too slow to admit a mistake and sell.

q: A stock has soared and everyone you know is sure it's going higher. Is this a good moment to buy?
why: When a stock looks great to everyone, most people who could buy it already have. That is when it is often near a top, and when discipline matters most.

q: Of the stocks that look exciting while you watch prices move, do more than half fail a full check of the criteria?
why: Price action alone grabs attention, but most of those stocks turn out mediocre once you check earnings and the other criteria. First look at a weekly chart, then do the full check.

q: Does the market often show its true strength or weakness in the last hour of the trading day?
why: Activity tends to slow around midday in New York. The final hour frequently reveals whether buyers are in control and the day closes strong, or whether early gains fade.

q: A company reports a bad quarter and its stock rises. Does that mean the market got it wrong?
why: The bad news was often expected and already priced in. Some professionals buy, or close short positions, once the bad news is finally out.

q: In late December, some weak stocks suddenly look strong. Is that a reliable sign of new market leaders?
why: Year-end trading is distorted by tax-driven selling and buying. Poor stocks can look strong for a while as former leaders rest. In time the true leaders show themselves again.

q: Can a very smart investor with an advanced degree still lose a lot of money by arguing with the market?
why: Intelligence and education are no guarantee in stocks. The market doesn't care what you think, and trying to prove you're right while it says otherwise is ego, which costs money.

q: Stocks that already rose the most over 1, 3 and 6 months feel too late. Does this approach skip them when scanning?
why: No. The scan looks for exactly those: the top 1 % to 2 % of stocks by gain over one, three and six months. That is how you find today's leaders.

q: Among all the factors in this momentum method, is liquidity, the money traded in a stock each day, the most important one?
why: Yes. Liquidity ranks first. The scans start from a minimum amount of money traded per day, before any chart is judged.

q: A stock trades about $5 million worth of shares a day. Does it pass a minimum liquidity scan of $20 million a day?
why: No. The scan requires at least $20 million traded per day, and $80 million for the most liquid list. At $5 million, the stock is too thin.

q: Is building your own database of past big movers' charts, over hundreds of hours, part of finding a trading edge?
why: Yes. The advice is to go through the charts of past movers, decades back, save the patterns that repeat, and study them for at least a few hundred hours before trading them.

q: During earnings season, does the pre-market routine include checking which stocks are gapping up on their reports?
why: Yes. In earnings season the routine adds a check for earnings winners gapping up, before the regular scan for big gappers and the news behind them.
